turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Room three is open whenever you're ready. Umm, sorry for the wait, the lot was jammed with that paving on Maple.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. The interstate was quite slow as well, so I gave myself extra time.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Oh I know. I sat through three lights by the mall. They keep saying the work wraps up Friday if it doesn't rain.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I do hope the forecast holds. It has made the mornings rather trying.

[SEG0005] person_3 (NURSE): Hey, I'll grab vitals before Dr. Shah comes in. I'm his sister, I work this clinic on Thursdays. Blood pressure is 132 over 78, pulse 118, respirations 16, oxygen 99 percent, temperature 36.9 Celsius.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning. I'm Dr. Shah. Tell me what made you come in.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. I am 29. I have been losing weight, and my heart races even when I am sitting quietly.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mm. How much weight have you dropped, and any sweating, shaky hands, or eating more or less?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): About twelve pounds, I would say. I sweat more than before, my hands shake, and I am eating more than usual.
[SEG0010] person_3 (NURSE): It's been three months of this. And he barely sleeps, I've watched it at the house.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): If I may, the weight loss is closer to six weeks, not three months. And I do sleep, only more lightly than I used to. I would not say I barely sleep.

[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, so err, somewhere between six weeks and three months, and the sleep is lighter rather than gone. Let me think this through. When the thyroid puts out too much hormone it revs up metabolism, so you can lose weight even while eating more, and it drives the heart faster and makes the hands tremble. I'm wondering about an overactive thyroid.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister does have thyroid disease, doctor. The symptoms themselves are what brought me in, though.
[SEG0014] person_3 (NURSE): Yeah, they told me Graves back in college. My little boy tries to sneak the white pill like it's a mint, which is its own headache at home.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Useful context, but we'll go by your labs, not hers. Any ongoing medical problems of your own?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I have asthma. I have had it since I was a child. I use an albuteral inhaler, two puffs when I need it.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever with all this?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): And with the asthma, have you been wheezing?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, if I hurry on the stairs.

[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay, sometimes on the stairs, not constant. Uh, let me look. Fine tremor in both hands, yeah that fits. Thyroid feels a little full, rhythm is regular, and the lungs are clear with no wheeze right now.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Do you think it is serious?

[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can't say for certain today. My working impression is hyperthyroidism, provisional, from the weight loss, the fast heart, the sweating, the tremor, eating more, and your sister's thyroid disease. We'll get a TSH and a free T4, and an EKG while you're here.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. Is there anything I should do in the meantime?

[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ease off the caffeine, coffee and those energy drinks, until we know more. Keep the albuterol if you wheeze. I'll see you back in one week to go over the results. If you faint or get real chest pain, go to the emergency room.
[SEG0030] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can book the EKG down the hall and the blood draw right after, and I'll put that one-week visit on the schedule.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I appreciate all of your help. Thank you.

spec.situation: Younger adult losing weight with a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaky hands, eats more than usual; hair thinning not mentioned; a sister has thyroid disease; blood tests and ECG planned.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.reason: Patient said 'not really,' not a definite absence.
Doctor advised ER for fainting or real chest pain; fact omits 'real' chest pain detail.
bad.text: Go to the emergency room if fainting or chest pain (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

Chest pain was recorded as absent, but the patient answered 'Not really,' which is not a clear denial.
Physical exam also documented lungs clear on auscultation.
